extracted.intended_audience: academic authors submitting manuscripts to scholarly journals (particularly early career researchers)
extracted.subtask_short: avoiding desk rejection for journal articles
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for researchers preparing and submitting a journal article to avoid immediate (desk) rejection by editors. Covers choosing an appropriate journal, preparing a manuscript that meets journal expectations, and following ethical and procedural requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sent to the wrong journal
rubrics_metrics.description: Choosing a journal that is not a good fit for your work can slow down the publishing process and lead to desk rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read a lot of published research to identify journals that publish work similar to yours; note journals when you find comparable articles. Talk to colleagues and mentors for recommendations. Use tools such as the Taylor & Francis Journal Suggester (which reviews your abstract and pairs it with suitable journals). After identifying candidate journals, read each journal’s aims and scope statement to confirm the types of research they publish and whether your work fits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not a true journal article
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors may determine the submission is not a true journal article but rather another type of academic writing (e.g., book chapter, condensed thesis) and reject it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for characteristics that make a submission look unlike a journal article: has many different points; is unfocused; is too journalistic; lacks the structure or language of a journal article. Before writing, spend time understanding your specific work and the audience you want to reach. Recognize that research can produce many types of outputs; choose the format appropriate for your content. Especially for early career researchers, present findings in the manner typical for your field. Ensure the article has the expected structure and level of focus for a journal submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not following the journal’s guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to follow a journal’s Instructions for Authors (IFAs) and submission requirements is an easy reason for desk rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Get familiar with the target journal’s IFAs, which specify article preparation requirements, manuscript submission process, publishing options (e.g., open access), the peer review process, data sharing policy, and other expectations. By reading the IFAs you can determine whether your article is ready for submission according to the journal’s expectations and whether it includes everything the editorial board expects. Adhere to formatting, length, referencing, and policy requirements listed in the IFAs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unsound manuscript
rubrics_metrics.description: A manuscript may be considered unsound if it fails on quality, presentation, contribution, or fit with journal conventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common reasons an editor labels a manuscript unsound include: poor regard for the journal’s conventions; inadequate style, grammar, punctuation, or English; no contribution to the subject; not properly contextualized; lacking an appropriate theoretical framework; messy presentation and sloppy proofreading. To avoid this: read well-written articles in your field to learn structure and presentation; treat the paper as a story with consistent flow; complete a full draft before heavy editing; revise and proofread carefully. Share drafts with appropriate colleagues for feedback and fresh eyes to catch mistakes; submit the manuscript only when it is in the best possible shape.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unethical, or lacks objectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Breaches of ethical guidelines or presentation of research in a problematic way can cause immediate rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of common ethical issues include authorship disputes; undeclared competing interests; duplicate submission/publication; fabrication or falsification of data or images; plagiarism or text recycling; and copyright breaches. Many such problems arise from misunderstanding or confusion about policies. Authors should consult the journal’s ethics guidance (e.g., the 'ethics for journal authors' guide), use available ethical checklists, and seek guidance/support where unclear. The page also references a related webinar for more insights on avoiding rejection.
